You hand it over, or set it down, or let somebody else carry it, and you sleep. That is not distance from your life. It is contact with something that grew until it was ready to leave your hands.

What makes it work is that you are not managing the outcome while the thing goes. You let it change shape once it is out of the room. Others keep checking what it becomes; you know how to stop checking. Keep the same attention on what you are now, piece by piece, without asking it to prove it deserves the space.
1.sheetLine: You let go when it is done, because it is done.

2.tense: You are already packing up the room before the last thing has been said in it.
2.verb: Letting go of what you have finished with
2.place: Where what you are becomes visible without being forced
2.ask: Pick one unfinished thing and say what is still missing for you, not for anyone else. Then stay with it until that part is done.
2.core:
You keep getting ahead of the nearness of endings. Before anything has really finished, you are already letting go, and it looks like maturity. But it is not the soft release of something complete. You call it letting go when you are avoiding the part where you would be present for the last step. It feels safer to leave early than to stand in a room that is still filling up.

Stay long enough to feel the weight of it. The practice is not to grip harder — it is to let the thing be unfinished until it is not, and to let yourself be seen in the meantime. Solitude with your own craft can steady you. It turns into a place to hide if you use it to disappear. Let one thing run its whole length. You will know the difference when it lands.
2.sheetLine: You are letting go too soon to avoid the ending.

3.tense: You are still holding something that finished before you noticed the door behind you.
3.verb: Letting go of what you have finished with
3.place: Where what you are becomes visible without being forced
3.ask: Pick the thing you are carrying hardest. Put it down for one hour, somewhere you can see it, and do not touch it.
3.core:
You are tired in a way that rest does not fix. Something in your life has ended, or changed, and you are still gripping it, still carrying the shape of it because letting go feels like losing. So you hold. You hold the old job, the old version of a person, the plan you made when things were different. None of it is alive anymore, and still you keep it up.

What would help is not more will. It is a little endurance spent differently, the kind that holds without crushing. You can set something down without throwing it away. Try letting a thing be as heavy as it is for one hour while you do nothing to fix it. The strength is already in you; it just needs somewhere to go that is not the same clenched grip.
3.sheetLine: You carry what has already gone, and it is heavy.

4.tense: You have been writing the ending without noticing that the pen has been in your hand the whole time.
4.verb: Letting go of what you have finished with
4.place: Where what you are becomes visible without being forced
4.ask: Say one thing you have already let go of, as a fact, in a plain sentence to one person. Do not explain it.
4.core:
You have already released something. That happened. But you describe it like it was done to you, or like it has not happened yet, so you keep checking for it. You may also be holding on to something and calling it steady. From the outside you cannot tell which one is true. What is missing is not another effort. It is recognizing which motion you are actually in.

Start smaller. Pay attention to what is growing, even the slow part, and do not force it into a shape. Look at one ordinary thing you do for someone and see the care in it. That is the same hand that lets go. You are not behind on this. You are already in it.
4.sheetLine: You have already let go. You just have not claimed it.

1.tense: You let go when the thing is finished, and you know the finish is the release.
1.verb: Letting go of what you've kept past its use
1.place: Standing back far enough to see the whole shape while still inside it
1.ask: Name one thing you put down this month, out loud, to someone who'll hear it plain. Then put your care on what's still growing.
1.core:
You can see the whole shape of something while you're still inside it. A thing is running and you can tell what it's for, where it's going, what to keep. And the release is flowing. Things finish and you let them finish — no fighting the ending, no propping it open with your back.

That kind of letting go isn't defeat. It's how the next thing gets room. Your care here is the kind that doesn't grip, so you hold what's growing loosely enough that it can move, and you're not worn out doing it. So the question is small. Say it out loud once: what did you put down this month. Then put the care on what's actually growing now, and let that be the weight you're under.
1.sheetLine: You release things when they're done, and the release is the point.

2.tense: You brace for an ending that hasn't arrived, and you surrender ahead of the actual finish.
2.verb: Letting go of what you've kept past its use
2.place: Standing back far enough to see the whole shape while still inside it
2.ask: Pick one open thing and leave it open for a week. No conclusion, no pre-emptive surrender, no calling it finished before it is.
2.core:
Somewhere ahead is a place where you've already given it up, and you're living back here as if that's done. You release before the thing is finished — hand it over, drop it, call it over — and what should be clearing becomes a way to get ahead of a loss you can feel coming.

Seeing the whole shape is usually a gift, and here it's the problem: you see the end so early you mistake it for now. The practice isn't more release. It's staying with something while it's still running, without forcing a close. Keep the small daily thing going. Not to fix anything, but to remind yourself the thing in front of you isn't over just because you can see where it goes.
2.sheetLine: You let go early, then call it finished to make the timing true.

3.tense: You are still gripping what's already over, holding weight from something that finished without you.
3.verb: Letting go of what you've kept past its use
3.place: Standing back far enough to see the whole shape while still inside it
3.ask: Name one thing you're carrying past its time. Then water a plant or keep one routine for a week, and let that be where the grip goes.
3.core:
You're carrying things that are over. Doors that closed behind you, and you're at them still — arranging, tending, doing the work of keeping what's already gone. The tiredness doesn't lift with rest, because the load finished and you're still under it.

Seeing the whole shape isn't the trouble here; the grip is. So don't try to let go by force. Letting go by force is just another grip. The way back is strength that doesn't crush, the kind that holds something worth holding without breaking it, practiced on a small living thing instead of an old done one. Water the plant. Keep the routine. Let that be where the weight goes, and let the rest get lighter on its own.
3.sheetLine: You're carrying things that finished, and the weight isn't the framed one.

4.tense: You have already put something down, and you keep describing it as still in your hands.
4.verb: Letting go of what you've kept past its use
4.place: Standing back far enough to see the whole shape while still inside it
4.ask: Pick one thing you say is still open. Say what's actually true about it now. Then care for one thing that's growing, no force, no clutching.
4.core:
You can watch yourself and the room at the same time, which means you usually catch what's happening. But somewhere here you've stopped catching one thing: you let it go, and you're still talking like you're the one holding it. Or you think you released it and the grip is still there. Either way the hand is doing something the story hasn't caught up to.

That's not a flaw, it's a lag. Your read on the pattern is running; the admitting isn't. So the act is simple: say what's true about one open thing, without deciding whether it should be closed. Then put care somewhere — a thing that's growing, tended without forcing. That care is where the surrender gets visible, instead of a claim you keep making about yourself.
4.sheetLine: Your hands already let go. Your story hasn't caught up.

1.tense: Release is moving through your days without needing to be pushed.
1.verb: letting go of what no longer holds
1.place: the point where the work is done and the next thing begins
1.ask: Take the task you keep almost-finishing, do its last hour today, and mark it done on paper.
1.core:
Endings come out of your hands clean right now. You close something and the closing itself makes room — not staring at the door, not holding it shut. That's rare, and it's doing quiet work: new things have somewhere to land because the old ones aren't still sitting in your lap.

What keeps this is tending without clutching. A plant doesn't need you standing over it; it needs water, light, and then your absence. Give what you've made what it needs to hold up on its own, then step back and let it be enough. The test isn't whether you feel finished. It's whether you can stop working on something and let the next thing show up in its own time, without earning the right to rest first.
1.sheetLine: You can close a thing and mean it.

2.tense: You will be handing it off before it is finished, once the moment comes.
2.verb: letting go of what no longer holds
2.place: the point where the work is done and the next thing begins
2.ask: Take the project you keep wanting to hand off early, work twenty unhurried minutes on it alone tomorrow, then stop on purpose.
2.core:
You're jumping to the ending before the middle is done. Somewhere ahead is the version where it's over and you're already living there — announcing it, passing it on, releasing something that still needs your hands. The gesture reads as trust from the outside. From the inside, it's a sprint past the part that would require you to sit still and finish.

What turns this is quiet practice: twenty minutes, no audience, repetition instead of announcement. Keep one small light on rather than torching it. If you can work without a witness, the thing gets to be whole before you offer it up. Releasing it isn't the problem. Doing it before the work is ready is.
2.sheetLine: You hand things off before they're done and call it trust.

3.tense: You were carrying it then, and your hands have not opened since.
3.verb: letting go of what no longer holds
3.place: the point where the work is done and the next thing begins
3.ask: Pick one thing you're keeping alive past its time, hold it deliberately for five minutes, then set it down for an hour and watch your body do it.
3.core:
Something is being carried that's ready to be put down. The grip is tired — it shows in your shoulders before it shows in your words — and it keeps going, past the point where it was useful. Things that might have ended stay held open, and what's exhausted is you, not the thing.

Opening your hands for good isn't the move yet. The move is to grip one thing on purpose, so it becomes something you're doing rather than something happening to you. Five minutes of deliberate hold, then an hour of deliberate rest. Your body learns the difference between the two. One hour is enough to start, and starting is what makes the rest possible later.
3.sheetLine: You're still holding it, and your hands are the tired part.

4.tense: You have already put something down and you don't count it as done.
4.verb: letting go of what no longer holds
4.place: the point where the work is done and the next thing begins
4.ask: Find one thing you say you still have to do, and write one sentence on whether you stopped doing it or already finished it.
4.core:
You speak of it as still open. Look at what you actually reach for and what you quietly stopped reaching for — the answer is already there, and you've been living it while telling people you haven't decided. The message you didn't send, the person you stopped mentioning, the evening that no longer goes that way. Something was released without an announcement, and now you can't tell whether it ended or just went quiet.

Care for what's still growing means looking at what you do, not what you say you're waiting on. One sentence, written plainly, draws the line. The release already happened. Knowing it is the part you can add today.
4.sheetLine: You already put it down. You haven't written it down.
